The Personal Savings Allowance (PSA) gives basic-rate taxpayers £1,000/year of tax-free interest. Higher-rate taxpayers get £500. Additional-rate taxpayers get nothing. Beyond your PSA, Cash ISA wins decisively.

Cash ISA vs Taxable Savings — When Does It Matter?

For most basic-rate taxpayers with under £25,000 in savings, ordinary easy-access accounts often beat Cash ISAs because they pay slightly more interest and the PSA shields the first £1,000 of interest from tax. Above £25k or for higher-rate taxpayers, the ISA wrapper wins.

For long-term savings (5+ years), the question isn't "Cash ISA vs taxable savings" — it's "Cash ISA vs Stocks & Shares ISA." Equities historically deliver 4-5% above cash returns over multi-decade horizons.

The Compound Interest Formula

A = P(1 + r/n)nt

Where:

  • A = Final amount
  • P = Starting balance (principal)
  • r = Annual interest rate (decimal)
  • n = Compounding frequency per year
  • t = Time in years

Example: £10,000 at 4.5% AER compounded annually for 10 years. A = 10000 × (1.045)^10 = ~£15,530. Almost certainly beats cash under the bed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What's the Personal Savings Allowance?
Basic-rate taxpayers: £1,000/year of tax-free interest. Higher-rate: £500. Additional-rate: £0. Beyond your PSA, cash interest is taxed at your marginal rate.
FSCS protection?
£85,000 per person per FSCS-authorised institution. If you have more than £85k, spread across institutions to stay under the cap.
Are Premium Bonds worth it?
Average ~4.15% but you might win nothing. Best as a small tax-free portion of your savings if you like the optionality. Don't make them more than 10-20% of your cash savings unless you have very high holdings.
Fix vs easy-access?
Fixes typically pay 0.2-0.5% more for locking up money 1-2 years. Worth it for the portion you definitely won't need. Keep your emergency fund in easy-access regardless of the slight yield drag.
